A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same actor-network-based attack and safety-data construction work, despite substantial rewriting and renaming. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original HarmBench attack evaluations, sensitivity and safeguard analyses, and safety-fine-tuning experiments measuring safety and helpfulness.

after.justification: v2 retains original attack and fine-tuning results and reports additional actor-category, efficiency, defense and human-judgment experiments.

M1.justification: ActorAttack is renamed ActorBreaker, but the proposed network construction, attack-chain reasoning, self-talk, response handling and refusal-data construction procedures remain. Algorithm 1 retains the same steps. Dynamic modification is explicitly optional in v2, matching the variant already evaluated without it in v1.

E1.justification: The newly evaluated Multilingual attack adds language-transformed prompt conditions, consistent with the low-resource-language approach described in related work; specific languages are unspecified. HarmBench, the training-data sources and all four helpfulness benchmarks remain. GPT-o1 was already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds Multilingual, AutoDAN, ReNeLLM and CoA, and broadens Crescendo comparisons across target models. Table 8 adds Rephrase, RPO and Circuit Breaker defense comparisons. Conversely, Crescendo disappears from the fine-tuned-model safety table and turn-budget comparison, despite remaining elsewhere.

E3.justification: v2 introduces actor-category combination experiments, an interaction-count efficiency metric, and judge validation using majority voting over ten annotations per query. The larger SFT condition changes from 1000 to 1680 samples, although Appendix D.2 still describes collecting 1000 dialogues without reconciling these counts. This establishes revised reported settings, not that training was rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test individual actor categories and their combinations, interaction efficiency, robustness against existing defenses, and automatic judges against human evaluations. Actor-count sensitivity extends to Llama models. The MD-Judge safeguard analysis and standalone attack-path score distribution in v1 are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report three independent trials for prompt-diversity evaluation. Neither reports confidence intervals, significance tests or seed-based uncertainty estimates. The new human-annotation voting procedure changes evaluation design, without adding uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Claude-3.5 ASR changes from 66.5% to 78.5% with dynamic modification and from 54.5% to 65.5% without it; the other original Table 1 target scores and GPT-o1's 60% remain. v2 adds category, efficiency, defense and judge results and revises sensitivity results. Crescendo's post-SFT results are removed. Unspecified ablation settings prevent treating all numerical revisions as comparable performance gains.

T1.justification: The network formalization, conditional generation expressions and diversity equation remain unchanged. Expanded discussion of actor-network theory provides conceptual motivation rather than new mathematical assumptions, derivations or proofs.

C1.justification: v2 redefines the central contribution as discovering vulnerability to natural distribution shifts involving benign prompts within the pre-training distribution. It adds an explicit efficiency-superiority claim and emphasizes broader semantic coverage in safety training. The earlier specific claim of safety generalization to unseen Crescendo attacks is no longer presented.

C2.justification: v2 interprets vulnerability through a pre-training versus safety-training distribution gap and reframes GPT-o1 examples as a chain-of-thought faithfulness concern. It adds interpretations of actor-category coverage, CoA topic drift, judge errors and defense mechanisms. The English-only scope, prospective multimodal extension and safety–helpfulness trade-off remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies GPT-4o as the attack model and explains that attacker, judge and monitor roles use the same LLM with different instructions. It changes the stated code location and removes the direct SafeMTData link and 50-example ablation-sampling description. LoRA hyperparameters and helpfulness-evaluation details are largely retained in Appendix D.2.

R1.justification: Related work substantially repositions existing multi-turn attacks as exploiting malicious distribution shifts, contrasting them with the authors' claimed natural shifts. New citations and discussion include Red Queen, CFA, RPO and chain-of-thought faithfulness studies. Publication updates and the relocated defense survey do not themselves constitute new positioning.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and research narrative are substantially rewritten, and ActorAttack becomes ActorBreaker. Method explanations expand, results are reorganized, and the separate safety-fine-tuning section is distributed between experiments and appendices. Limitations and ethics become standalone sections.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws Figures 1 and 3, separates dynamic-modification results from the main comparison table, and replaces the combined budget/diversity display with separate tables. New analysis tables and redistributed appendix figures substantially change visual organization; the five detailed dialogue examples are retained.

improvement.justification: Actor-category tests and broader attack/defense comparisons strengthen empirical support and reveal useful failure boundaries beyond v1. The net gain is limited by removed Crescendo safety-generalization evidence and reporting problems: the 1680-sample condition is not reconciled with 1000 collected dialogues, Section 4.2 misquotes Table 1 averages, and Table 10 contains an incorrect judge–human difference. The stronger distributional framing also exceeds what the experiments directly establish.
